pumac-2023-geometry-b-01.title: Inradius and coordinates
pumac-2023-geometry-b-01.body:
$\triangle ABC$ is a $7$-$24$-$25$ right triangle, so $r=\frac{\text{area}}{s}=\frac{\frac12\cdot7\cdot24}{28}=3$ (or $r=\frac{7+24-25}2=3$). $\triangle CDA$ is congruent, so its inradius is also $3$.

Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(24,0)$, $C=(24,7)$, $D=(0,7)$. The incenter of $\triangle ABC$ (right angle at $B$) is $(24-3,3)=(21,3)$; the incenter of $\triangle CDA$ (right angle at $D$) is $(3,7-3)=(3,4)$. So $d^2=(21-3)^2+(3-4)^2=324+1=325$.

**Answer: 325**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-02.title: Centered square, tilt angle $15^\circ$
pumac-2023-geometry-b-02.body:
The largest square can be taken centered at the hexagon's center $O$ (the hexagon is convex and centrally symmetric). Let its half-diagonal be $\rho$ and let one vertex make angle $\varphi$ with a direction pointing to a hexagon *vertex*; vertices of the square point in directions $\varphi,\varphi+90^\circ,\dots$.

A point at distance $\rho$ in a direction making angle $\delta$ with the nearest apothem direction is inside the hexagon (apothem $\frac{\sqrt3}2$) iff $\rho\cos\delta\le\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Apothem directions are $30^\circ+60^\circ j$, and the four square vertices make angles $\varphi,\varphi+30^\circ,\varphi,\varphi+30^\circ$ with the vertex directions mod $60^\circ$, so (for $0\le\varphi\le30^\circ$) their angular distances $\delta$ to the nearest apothem direction are $30^\circ-\varphi$ and $\varphi$. We need $\rho\le\frac{\sqrt3/2}{\cos\delta}$ for both, and the better of the two constraints is best balanced when $\varphi=15^\circ$, giving $\delta=15^\circ$ for all four vertices:
$$\rho=\frac{\sqrt3/2}{\cos15^\circ}.$$
The area of a square with half-diagonal $\rho$ is $2\rho^2=\dfrac{3/2}{\cos^215^\circ}=\dfrac{3}{1+\cos30^\circ}=\dfrac{6}{2+\sqrt3}=6(2-\sqrt3)=12-6\sqrt3.$

So $a+b+c=12+6+3=21$. (The side is $3-\sqrt3\approx1.27$.)

**Answer: 21**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-03.title: Pythagoras on each pair
pumac-2023-geometry-b-03.body:
If the common chord of circles of radii $r_i<r_j$ is a diameter of the smaller one, the segment from the center $O_i$ to an endpoint $T$ of the chord has length $r_i$, the center $O_j$ also is at distance $r_j$ from $T$, and $O_iO_j$ is perpendicular to the chord (which passes through $O_i$). So $O_iO_j^2=r_j^2-r_i^2$.

The side lengths of the triangle of centers satisfy $O_1O_2^2=25-9=16$, $O_1O_3^2=49-9=40$, $O_2O_3^2=49-25=24$. Since $16+24=40$, it is a right triangle with legs $\sqrt{16}=4$ and $\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt6$, so the area is $4\sqrt6$ and the square of the area is $96$.

**Answer: 96**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-04.title: Embed in an equilateral triangle
pumac-2023-geometry-b-04.body:
The height from $A$ is $\sqrt{7-\frac14}=\frac{3\sqrt3}2$, which is the height of an equilateral triangle of side $3$. So extend $BC$ to the equilateral triangle $AXY$ of side $3$ with $B,C$ the trisection points of $XY$; $G$ (at distance $\frac23$ of the height from $A$) is also the center of $AXY$. A rotation by $120^\circ$ about $G$ maps $AXY$ to itself ($A\to X\to Y\to A$), so $T_0,T_1,T_2\subset AXY$, and each $T_j$ is the part of $AXY$ cut out by the two cevians from one vertex to the trisection points of the opposite side.

Take $M,N$ on $AY,AX$ with $AM:MY=AN:NX=1:2$. Let $P'=AB\cap MX$, $R=AC\cap NY$, $Q=NY\cap MX$. By $3$-fold symmetry, the region is $3$ congruent kites $P'QRG$: $K=3[P'QRG]$. The kite has perpendicular diagonals $P'R$ (parallel to $XY$) and $QG$ (on the axis through $A$), so $[P'QRG]=\frac12\,P'R\cdot QG$.

With mass points: $AP':P'B=3:2$, so $P'R=\frac35BC=\frac35$ (similar triangles $AP'R\sim ABC$). The point $Q$ lies at half the height of $AXY$ from $A$ (by mass points on the cevians $MX,NY$), i.e. $AQ=\frac{3\sqrt3}4$, so $QG=AG-AQ=\sqrt3-\frac{3\sqrt3}4=\frac{\sqrt3}4$. Hence
$$K=3\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}4=\frac{9\sqrt3}{40},\qquad K^2=\frac{243}{1600},$$
and $a+b=243+1600=1843$.

(Coordinates confirm this: with $G$ the origin, $A=(0,\sqrt3)$, $X=(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$, one finds $P'=(-0.3,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{10})$, $R=(0.3,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{10})$, $Q=(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}4)$.)

**Answer: 1843**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-05.title: Opposite edges are equal (disphenoid)
pumac-2023-geometry-b-05.body:
The edges of the tetrahedron $DEFG$ are $DE=\frac{AC}2=7.5$, $EF=\frac{AB}2=6.5$, $DF=\frac{BC}2=7$, and the folded edges $GD=AD=6.5$, $GE=BE=7$, $GF=AF=7.5$. So opposite edges are equal: $DE=GF=7.5$, $EF=GD=6.5$, $DF=GE=7$. Such a tetrahedron fits in a rectangular box $p\times q\times r$ with its edges as face diagonals:
$$p^2+q^2=6.5^2,\quad q^2+r^2=7^2,\quad r^2+p^2=7.5^2 .$$
Adding and solving: $p^2=\frac{42.25+56.25-49}2=\frac{99}4$, $q^2=\frac{42.25+49-56.25}2=\frac{35}2$, $r^2=\frac{49+56.25-42.25}{2}=\frac{63}2$. The tetrahedron is the box minus four corner pieces each of volume $\frac16pqr$, so $V=\frac13pqr$.
$$pqr=\sqrt{\tfrac{99}4\cdot\tfrac{35}2\cdot\tfrac{63}2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{218295}{16}}=\frac{63\sqrt{55}}4,\qquad V=\frac{21\sqrt{55}}4.$$
So $p+q+r=21+55+4=80$.

**Answer: 80**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-05.title: Dihedral angle
pumac-2023-geometry-b-05.body:
Let $H_1,H_2$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and from $E$ to $DF$ in the original plane. Since $\triangle ADF$ and $\triangle EFD$ are half-size copies of the $13$-$14$-$15$ triangle (area $84$), $AH_1=EH_2=6$, $DH_1=FH_2=\frac52$, $H_1H_2=2$. After folding, $GE=BE=7$ and $G$ projects onto the plane perpendicular to $DF$ so that $G'E'=\sqrt{7^2-2^2}=\sqrt{45}$. The law of cosines in $\triangle G'H'E'$ (sides $6,6,\sqrt{45}$) gives the dihedral angle $\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\frac38$, so the height of $G$ above plane $DEF$ is $6\sin\theta=\frac{3\sqrt{55}}4$. With $[DEF]=\frac{84}4=21$, $V=\frac13\cdot21\cdot\frac{3\sqrt{55}}4=\frac{21\sqrt{55}}4$.

**Answer: 80**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-06.title: $AX=AM$
pumac-2023-geometry-b-06.body:
The circle centered at $M$ through $B$ also passes through $C$ (since $MB=MC$), and $MB^2=MD\cdot MA$ (from $\triangle MBD\sim\triangle MAB$). The perpendicular bisector of $DM$ is perpendicular to $AM$, so $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric about line $AM$ (the circle is too), hence $AX=AY$.

For $X$: $XD=XM$ (it is on the perpendicular bisector) and $XM=MB$. So $MX^2=MD\cdot MA$ and $\angle XMD=\angle AMX$, giving $\triangle MXD\sim\triangle MAX$, so $\frac{AX}{XD}=\frac{MA}{MX}$, and as $XD=MX$ we get $AX=AM$.

Thus $AX\cdot AY=AM^2$. In a triangle with $a=6$, $b=5$, $c=4$ we have $a^2=36=c(c+b)$, which holds exactly when $\angle A=2\angle C$. Then $\angle ACM=\angle C+\frac A2=A$ and $AM=2R\sin(\angle ACM)=2R\sin A=BC=6$. So $AX\cdot AY=36$.

**Answer: 36**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-07.title: Homothety at $A$
pumac-2023-geometry-b-07.body:
Since $DE\parallel BC$, $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle ABC$ by a homothety $h$ centered at $A$ taking $D\to B$, $E\to C$. It maps $\omega=(ADE)$ to the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of $ABC$, so $\omega$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $\omega$ is tangent to $BC$ at some $X$ whose image $M=h(X)$ lies on $\Gamma$ and on line $AX$, with tangent parallel to $BC$ at $M$: so $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$, and $AX$ bisects $\angle BAC$. The ratio of $h$ is $\frac{AX}{AM}=\frac{DE}{BC}$.

- Angle bisector theorem: $BX:XC=15:20$, so $BX=9$, $XC=12$. Stewart's theorem: $AX^2\cdot21+9\cdot12\cdot21=15^2\cdot12+20^2\cdot9$, giving $AX^2=192$, $AX=8\sqrt3$.
- $\cos A=\frac{15^2+20^2-21^2}{2\cdot15\cdot20}=\frac{23}{75}$. In $\triangle BMC$, $\angle BMC=180^\circ-A$ and $BM=CM$, so $21^2=2BM^2(1+\cos A)=BM^2\cdot\frac{196}{75}$, i.e. $BM=\frac{15\sqrt3}2$. Ptolemy in $ABMC$: $AM\cdot21=BM(AB+AC)=BM\cdot35$, so $AM=\frac{25\sqrt3}2$.

Therefore $DE=BC\cdot\frac{AX}{AM}=21\cdot\frac{8\sqrt3}{25\sqrt3/2}=\frac{336}{25}$, and $a+b=361$.

**Answer: 361**

pumac-2023-geometry-b-08.title: Spiral similarity
pumac-2023-geometry-b-08.body:
$\triangle AB'C'$ is the image of $\triangle ABC$ under the spiral similarity centered at $A$ with angle $\frac{5\pi}{12}$ and ratio $\frac{\sqrt6}2$ (all sides are scaled by $\frac{7\sqrt6}{14}=\frac{\sqrt6}2$). A standard property: $D=BB'\cap CC'$ lies on both circumcircles $(ABC)$ and $(AB'C')$. Hence $O$ is the circumcenter of $ABC$ and $O'$ that of $AB'C'$, and the same spiral similarity takes $O$ to $O'$: $AO'=\frac{\sqrt6}2AO$ and $\angle OAO'=\frac{5\pi}{12}$.

Circumradius of $ABC$: Heron, $s=42$, area $=\sqrt{42\cdot28\cdot12\cdot2}=168$, $R=\frac{14\cdot30\cdot40}{4\cdot168}=25$. In $\triangle OAO'$ the law of cosines gives
$$OO'^2=25^2\left(1+\tfrac32-2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt6}2\cos75^\circ\right)=625\left(\tfrac52-\sqrt6\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}4\right)=625\cdot\frac{2+\sqrt3}{2},$$
and since $\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}2\right)^2=\frac{2+\sqrt3}2$, $OO'=\frac{25+25\sqrt3}2$. So $a+b+c+d=25+25+3+2=55$.

**Answer: 55**
